extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, journalists, and general readers interested in media studies and social movements
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing media coverage of social movements
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and criteria for analyzing how mainstream news media represent, shape, and manage activist movements — tracing processes such as framing, celebrity conversion, rhetorical inflation, and containment. Useful for scholarly critique, journalism studies, and activist media strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial ignoring, selection, and emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: "the media first ignore new political developments, then select and emphasize aspects of the story that treat movements as oddities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether coverage initially overlooks emerging movement activity, and if/when it begins coverage, what aspects editors/reporters select to highlight. Look for patterns that present movements as anomalous or marginal rather than as legitimate political actors; consider timing (delay of attention) and choice of imagery or anecdotes that exoticize or trivialize the movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and the struggle over images
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters and headings such as "The Struggle over Images," "Framing an Action," and "Identifying SDS" emphasize how journalists and outlets construct particular versions of a movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the frames applied (e.g., disorderly protest, legitimate grievance, extremist fringe) and how specific events are framed to produce lasting images. Examine who gets described as representative, which events become emblematic, and how competing frames (movement self-presentation vs. media frame) play out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifying leaders and converting leadership to celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Certifying Leaders and Converting Leadership to Celebrity" — including subthemes: The Manufacture of Celebrity; The Vulnerability of Ambivalent Leaders; Celebrity as Resource/ Career/ Trap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how media attention can elevate particular individuals into public celebrities, how that process shapes their behavior and accountability, and how celebrity status may estrange leaders from grassroots bases. Look for selection of spokespersons, personalization of movements, and the careerizing effects of media attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflating rhetoric and militancy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Inflating Rhetoric and Militancy" (e.g., 'The New Left Turns to Mood of Violence', 'Revolutionary Will and Action News', 'The Aestheticizing of Violence in Films').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether coverage amplifies militant or revolutionary language and imagery beyond its prevalence in the movement, potentially aestheticizing or normalizing violence. Consider headlines, footage selection, and editorial choices that may exaggerate militancy and thus affect public perceptions and internal movement dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevating moderate alternatives / promoting moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Elevating Moderate Alternatives: The Moment of Reform" and discussion of the Tet Crisis, 'Media on a Tightrope', and 'extraordinary measures to secure moderating frames.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate tendencies in coverage to legitimize moderate or reformist leaders/options while marginalizing radical alternatives. Look for disproportionate attention to compromise actors, use of 'moderate' frames, and editorial routines that privilege containment-oriented solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting time and eclipsing context (decontextualization)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Contracting Time and Eclipsing Context" — 'On Discontinuity and the Decontextualization of Experience.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether news coverage compresses complex histories and contexts into isolated episodes, creating a sense of discontinuity. Check for lack of background, omission of causal sequences, and presentation of events as sudden or inexplicable rather than part of longer processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting as containment
rubrics_metrics.description: "Broadcasting and Containment" — the idea that media broadcasting can function to contain movements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze ways in which the act of broadcasting (selection of images, timing, narrative closure) serves to neutralize, domesticate, or contain the disruptive potential of movements. Consider editorial strategies that channel dissent into manageable formats or spectacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media routines, stereotypes, and news organizational practices
rubrics_metrics.description: TOC items such as 'Media Routines and Political Crises', 'Routines and Stereotypes', and 'On Analyzing News' point to routine journalistic practices shaping coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how organizational routines (beats, sourcing habits, deadlines, reliance on official sources) and stereotyped story forms influence the selection and presentation of movement news. Look for formulaic narratives, reliance on established sources, and routine constraints that bias coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological hegemony as a process in journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ideological Hegemony as a Process" and 'The Workings of Hegemony in Journalism' with attention to the 'Limits of Hegemonic Routine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how journalism participates in broader hegemonic processes that naturalize certain political orders and marginalize oppositional voices. Assess mechanisms (framing, sourcing, expert selection) by which journalistic practice reproduces dominant ideologies and where those routines break down or are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for movement organization and internal dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Part II chapters on 'Organizational Crisis,' 'The Membership Surge and Prairie Power,' 'The Vulnerability of Ambivalent Leaders,' and implications such as 'From Community to Mass Movement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how media representation affects movement internal organization: leadership choices, membership surges or declines, internal divisions, and the transformation from grassroots to mass movement. Look for evidence that coverage alters recruitment, tactics, or internal legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case studies and historical contextualization as analytic method
rubrics_metrics.description: The book uses detailed case studies (SDS coverage, Chicago 1968, Tet crisis, anti-nuclear movements) and an Appendix on Sources and Methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims about media effects, require careful historical/contextual evidence: sourcing practices, interviews, and documented episodes. Treat case-study depth and methodological transparency as criteria for assessing analytic robustness.
